data.intent: Get fully prepared for a fintech job interview next week: a day-by-day plan, company and industry research, practice questions, behavioral stories, logistics, and focus tools.

suggestions.title: 7-day prep plan
suggestions.reason: A day-by-day roadmap so the week before the interview is structured, not scrambled

content.text: Interview prep: 7-day plan
Goal: walk in knowing the company, the role, and my own stories cold. Adjust the days to match the interview date.
Days 1-2: Research
Read the job description and highlight the top 5 requirements
Fill in the company research brief
Look up my interviewers on LinkedIn
Days 3-4: Skills and domain
Review core fintech concepts (payments, KYC/AML, compliance, ledgers)
Do 3 technical or case practice problems relevant to the role
Work through the practice question bank
Days 5-6: Stories and mock interviews
Write 5-6 STAR stories
Do a full mock interview out loud with a friend or a recording
Prepare 5 thoughtful questions to ask the interviewers
Day 7: Light review and logistics
Skim notes once, then stop cramming
Confirm time, location or video link, and outfit
Sleep early

suggestions.title: Interview rounds
suggestions.reason: Track each round, interviewer, format, and prep status in one place

suggestions.title: Company research brief
suggestions.reason: Structured research on the company, its products, market, and risks

content.text: Company research brief
What they do
One-sentence summary of the product, who it serves (consumers, SMBs, banks, enterprises), and how the company makes money.
Business model and metrics
Revenue streams (interchange, subscriptions, interest, SaaS fees)
Funding stage, investors, and latest round
Key metrics they would care about (TPV, ARPU, churn, fraud rate)
Competitors and positioning
List 3 direct competitors and what makes this company different.
Regulation and risk
Which licenses or regulators apply (e.g. money transmitter, banking partner, SEC, CFPB)? Any recent compliance news?
Recent news
Latest product launch or announcement
Latest funding, partnership, or leadership change
How I can contribute
Connect 2-3 of my past wins directly to their current priorities.

suggestions.reason: Log likely questions, rate confidence, and track which ones you have rehearsed

suggestions.reason: A study checklist of domain terms interviewers commonly probe

suggestions.title: STAR story bank
suggestions.reason: Prepared behavioral stories you can adapt to any question

content.text: STAR stories
Aim for 5-6 stories, each about 2 minutes spoken, with a measurable result. Each one should flex to several questions.
Story 1: Led through ambiguity
Situation:
Task:
Action:
Result (with numbers):
Story 2: Conflict or disagreement
Situation:
Task:
Action:
Result:
Story 3: A failure and what I learned
Situation:
Task:
Action:
Result and lesson:
Story 4: Working with risk, data, or compliance
Pick an example showing care with money, sensitive data, or regulated processes. This is especially relevant in fintech.

suggestions.title: Questions to ask them
suggestions.reason: Thoughtful questions for each interviewer show real interest and help you evaluate the role

content.text: Questions to ask
Role and team
What would success look like in the first 90 days?
How is the team structured and how does it work with compliance and risk?
Company and strategy
How is changing regulation shaping the roadmap?
What is the biggest challenge the company faces over the next year?
Process
What are the next steps and expected timeline?

suggestions.title: Interview day checklist
suggestions.reason: Logistics and last-minute reminders so nothing gets forgotten on the day

content.text: Interview day checklist
Night before
Lay out outfit and test video, audio, and charger
Print or open resume, job description, and notes
Confirm interviewer names and meeting link or address
Morning of
Eat, hydrate, and do a 10-minute warm-up of my intro pitch
Arrive or log in 10 minutes early
After
Send thank-you emails within 24 hours
Write down what went well and what to improve

suggestions.title: Campaign brief
suggestions.reason: One source of truth for goals, audience, messaging and the six-week phasing around the 14 Nov launch

content.text: Six-week launch campaign brief

Runs 19 Oct to 29 Nov 2026. Product launch is 14 Nov 2026 (moved because the payments review slipped). Team: Sam (content and PR), Priya (video, launch lead), Alex (paid, analytics and billing setup).
Goals
Primary: qualified demo requests and free-trial signups from launch week onward
Secondary: grow newsletter and waitlist before launch
Awareness: earn press and podcast mentions around launch
Audience and messaging
Target: operations and finance leads at 50-500 person B2B companies. Core message: one clear problem we solve, one proof point, one call to action per piece.
Phasing
Weeks 1-2 (19 Oct - 1 Nov): Tease. Problem-led blog posts, waitlist email, podcast bookings.
Week 3 (2 - 8 Nov): Prime. Demo video, press release, launch email drafts, paid creative approved.
Week 4 (9 - 15 Nov): Launch on 14 Nov. Announcement across all channels, launch webinar.
Weeks 5-6 (16 - 29 Nov): Sustain. Case studies, podcast episodes, retargeting, results roundup.
Pre-flight checklist
Confirm total budget and split by channel
Agree on one tracking convention for UTM links
Lock the content calendar for weeks 1-3
Set weekly results review (Fridays)

content.text: Monthly landlord routine
Run through this list once a month. Reset the checkboxes at the start of each month.
1st – 5th: Rent
Add this month's charges to the Rent payments table
Confirm payments received and mark as Paid
Send friendly reminders to anyone not yet paid
Mid-month: Maintenance
Review open maintenance requests and follow up with vendors
Check smoke/CO detectors and furnace filters if due
End of month: Admin
Log expenses and upload receipts
Check the Documents register for leases or insurance expiring in the next 90 days
Note any lease renewals or rent increases to send

content.text: Move-in / move-out checklist

Move-out

Final walk-through compared against move-in photos
Keys returned
Deposit itemization sent within the legal deadline
Tenant status changed to Former
Notes
Record any damage, repairs needed or cleaning issues here before turning the unit.

data.title: Project Brief: Migrating the Team Wiki to PlexiiWrite

content.text: Purpose

This project moves our team wiki from [current wiki tool] into PlexiiWrite. The aim is to end up with one trusted place for team knowledge that is easier to find, easier to keep current, and easier to contribute to than what we have today. This brief sets out what we want from the move, what is and is not included, the rough sequence of work, and the main risks to manage.
Goals
Move all content we still need into PlexiiWrite without losing information, history that matters, or working links.
Use the move to clean up. Outdated, duplicate and abandoned pages should be archived or deleted instead of carried over.
Give the wiki a clear structure and ownership model so each section has a named person responsible for keeping it accurate.
Get the whole team working in PlexiiWrite by the cutover date, with the old wiki set to read-only and then retired.
Scope

In scope are all active pages and attachments in the current wiki, the top-level structure and naming conventions in PlexiiWrite, access and permission setup, redirecting or updating links that point to the old wiki, and a short guide to help the team get started.

Out of scope are rewriting content beyond what is needed to fix formatting, integrations with other tools unless they are already in daily use, and any redesign of how the team documents its work. Those can follow as separate efforts once the migration is stable.
Approach and timeline
Preparation, by [date]. Confirm the project owner ([owner name]), inventory the current wiki, decide what to keep, archive or delete, and check what import options PlexiiWrite supports.
Structure and pilot, by [date]. Set up the PlexiiWrite structure and permissions, then migrate one or two sections as a trial to find formatting and link problems early.
Full migration, by [date]. Move the remaining approved content, assign section owners, and review each section after it lands.
Cutover, on [date]. Announce the switch, set the old wiki to read-only, and share the getting-started guide.
Wrap-up, by [date]. Collect feedback, fix loose ends, and archive the old wiki once everyone confirms nothing is missing.
Risks
Content may lose formatting, images or attachments in transit. The pilot step is there to catch this, and each section owner should check their pages after migration.
Internal and external links to the old wiki may break. We should list the most-used links up front and keep the old wiki readable until they are fixed.
Permissions may be set too loosely or too tightly. Agree on who can view and edit each area before moving content, and test with a non-admin account.
The team may keep using the old wiki out of habit. A firm cutover date, a read-only old wiki and a visible owner for questions will help.
Clean-up may stall the project if every page becomes a debate. Set a simple rule, such as archiving anything nobody claims by a set date, and stick to it.
Open questions
Who signs off on the final cutover, and who decides what gets archived?
Does PlexiiWrite offer a bulk import from [current wiki tool], or will some of the move be manual?
Do we need to keep the old wiki's page history, or is a final archived copy enough?

content.text: Welcome

Welcome to the support team at [company name]. This guide covers what to expect in your first week, the tools you will use every day, and how we handle escalations. It is meant to be read once at the start and revisited whenever you are unsure what to do next.

You are not expected to know everything by the end of week one. You are expected to ask questions early, learn how our customers talk about our product, and get comfortable with the process for handing off work you cannot solve yourself. Good support is mostly clear thinking, careful reading, and honest communication, and all of those can be learned.
Your first week
The plan below is a suggested rhythm. Your buddy, [buddy name], and your manager, [manager name], will adjust it to fit your schedule.
Day one: orientation and access

Spend the first day getting set up and meeting people. Make sure you have working logins for every tool listed in the next section, and confirm you can see the team's shared inbox or queue. Meet your buddy, who will be your first point of contact for any question, however small. Read through this guide and the product overview in the knowledge base.
Days two and three: learn the product and shadow

Use the product the way a customer would. Sign up for a test account, work through the main flows, and note anything that confuses you, because it likely confuses customers too. Then shadow experienced agents. Read how they open a reply, how they ask for missing information, and how they close a conversation. Read a sample of recently resolved tickets, including a few that were escalated, to see what a good handoff looks like.
Day four: answer with a safety net

Start drafting replies to real tickets. Your buddy reviews each one before it goes out. Expect plenty of feedback on tone, accuracy, and completeness. That is the purpose of this stage, not a sign that something is wrong. Pick tickets from the simpler categories first, such as account questions and how-to requests.
Day five: reply independently and review

Begin sending replies on straightforward tickets without pre-approval, while your buddy spot-checks your work. At the end of the day, sit down with your manager to talk through what went well, what felt unclear, and what you want to learn next. Use that conversation to set goals for your second week.
The tools you will use
You will work in a small number of tools. Exact names and access steps are below; fill in or confirm each one with your manager.
The helpdesk, [helpdesk tool], is where all customer conversations live. Every ticket should have an owner, a status, and a category at all times.

The knowledge base, [knowledge base location], holds both customer-facing help articles and internal documentation. Search it before you reply to anything, and link customers to articles when they help.
Team chat, [chat tool], is for quick questions, coordination, and escalations. Use the channel [support channel] for general questions and [escalation channel] for urgent issues.
The internal admin or account lookup tool, [admin tool], lets you view customer accounts. Treat everything in it as confidential and only look up accounts you need for a ticket.
The issue tracker, [issue tracker], is where bugs and feature requests are logged for the product and engineering teams. You will link tickets to issues rather than relaying details by chat alone.

A few habits will serve you well in all of them. Keep your ticket statuses current so teammates can trust the queue. Write internal notes on tickets as you work, so anyone picking it up later can see what has been tried. Never paste customer data into a place it does not belong, such as a public channel or a personal document.
How we handle tickets
Before you think about escalation, most tickets can be resolved by following the same basic steps.
Read the whole message and any earlier history before replying. Many back-and-forth exchanges come from skipping this.
Work out what the customer is actually trying to do, which is sometimes different from what they asked.
Search the knowledge base and past tickets for a known answer.
Reply in plain language, with the answer first, then the steps, then what happens next.
If you need more information, ask for everything you need in a single message rather than one detail at a time.
Confirm the issue is resolved before closing, or set a clear expectation for follow-up.

Our target response and resolution times are [response-time targets]. When you cannot meet a target, tell the customer what is happening and when they can expect to hear from you, rather than going quiet.

On tone, be warm, direct, and specific. Apologise when we got something wrong, without over-apologising for things that were not our fault. Never promise something you cannot confirm, such as a fix date or a refund, unless you have the authority and the facts.
How we handle escalations

An escalation is a handoff to someone with more access, authority, or expertise than you have. Escalating is a normal, expected part of the job. What matters is that you do it at the right time and with enough information that the next person does not have to start over.
When to escalate
Escalate when any of the following apply.
The issue looks like a bug or outage that you cannot resolve with documented steps.
The request needs a decision outside your authority, such as an exception to policy, a refund above your limit of [refund or approval limit], or a contract question.
The customer reports a security concern, a data privacy issue, or possible unauthorised access to their account.

slides.title: How to Write a Good Bug Report
slides.notes: Welcome everyone. In the next few minutes we will cover what makes a bug report easy to act on, and give you a simple structure you can use every time.

slides.title: Why a good report matters
bullets: A clear report gets fixed sooner
Vague reports cause back-and-forth questions
Engineers can only fix what they can reproduce
Good reports help others spot duplicates
Your time writing it saves the whole team time
slides.notes: The person reading your report usually has none of your context. Every question they have to ask you is a delay. A few extra minutes up front is almost always the cheaper option for everyone.

slides.title: The anatomy of a strong report
bullets: A short, specific title
Steps to reproduce, numbered
Expected result
Actual result
Environment details
Evidence such as screenshots, logs or video
slides.notes: Walk through each part in order. Stress that expected versus actual is what turns a complaint into a bug, because it shows exactly where the product departs from what it should do.

slides.title: Write steps someone else can follow
bullets: Start from a known point, such as logging in
One action per step
Name the exact buttons, fields and values you used
Note whether it happens every time or only sometimes
Cut any step that is not needed to trigger the bug
slides.notes: Imagine handing the steps to a colleague who has never seen the screen. If they could get stuck, add detail. If a step does not change the outcome, remove it so the path is as short as possible.

slides.title: Before and after
bullets: Weak title: "Checkout broken"
Stronger title: "Checkout button does nothing after applying a discount code"
Weak body: "It doesn't work, please fix"
Stronger body: steps, expected, actual, environment, screenshot
Same bug, very different time to resolve
slides.notes: Use this slide to make the contrast concrete. Read the weak version aloud and ask the room what they would need to ask the reporter. Then show how the stronger version answers those questions in advance.

slides.title: Your checklist before you hit submit
bullets: Did I search for an existing report first?
Can someone reproduce this from my steps alone?
Are expected and actual results both stated?
Did I attach evidence and note the environment?
Is this one issue, not several bundled together?
slides.notes: Close by encouraging everyone to run through this checklist each time until it becomes habit. Invite questions, and point people to [where bug reports are filed] and [who to ask for help] for anything unclear.

Refund Policy FAQ

Can I get a refund if I change my mind?

Yes. If you ask for a refund within 30 days of your purchase, we will refund you in full.

What happens if I ask after 30 days?

Once the 30 days have passed, we do not offer refunds on monthly payments. You can cancel at any time to stop future charges, and your access continues until the end of the period you have already paid for.

Is the policy different for annual plans?

Yes. If you are on an annual plan, we refund the unused portion of your subscription on a pro rata basis. You are only charged for the time you actually had the service, and the rest goes back to you.

How does a pro rata refund work?

We divide your annual payment across the twelve months of the plan and refund the months you have not used. For example, if you cancel an annual plan after three months, you would receive a refund for the remaining nine months, which is three quarters of what you paid.

Does the 30-day full refund apply to annual plans too?

Yes. If you cancel an annual plan within 30 days of purchase, you receive a full refund rather than a pro rata one. After that point, the pro rata calculation applies.

How do I request a refund?

Contact our support team at [support email] and include the email address on your account. We will confirm your request and process any refund that is due within [number of business days] business days.

results.text:
## Key Findings

- **Browsers dominate memory.** Each browser is a full Chromium renderer process that never sleeps, using roughly 80 MB for a light page and 150-400 MB for heavy SPAs. Only the active desk is mounted, so cost depends on how many widgets sit on that one desk.
- **There is no viewport culling.** Every widget on the active desk stays fully mounted and live, whether it is on screen, panned away, or hidden. This makes compositing and pan/zoom jank worse on browser-heavy desks.
- **Risk climbs steeply with browser count.** Up to 3 browsers is comfortable; 9-15 causes real swap pressure and jank; 16+ risks renderer kills and blank browser widgets.
- **Live wires and the minimap are the main CPU hot paths.** Wire overlay does O(wires) DOM reads per frame during drags, and the minimap re-renders every widget as a live preview on each layout change. Both become noticeable at roughly 30-50+ wires or dense desks.
- **Other widgets are cheap.** Most non-browser widgets cost under 30 MB each, and portals are inexpensive because they render static miniatures.

## Top 3 Recommendations

1. **Suspend offscreen and hidden browsers.** Use an IntersectionObserver or pan/zoom-driven visibility check in `WebViewWidget` to mute, throttle, or unload browsers that are fully off screen or occluded, reloading them when they return. This addresses the biggest stability risk and the compositor jank.
2. **Viewport-cull the canvas.** Skip mounting widgets well outside the viewport, with a margin, so large desks only mount what is near view. Browsers benefit most.
3. **Warn when a desk holds many browsers.** Track the live webview count and show a gentle performance hint past roughly 8 browsers per desk, which is cheap to add and prevents the worst surprises.

**Purpose:** Plexii is a desktop app. The browser version has one job: letting someone who is sent a desk open it for 48 hours with no install or account, after which it is deleted. It is not a second edition and not a place to keep a workspace [1]. It runs the same renderer and data layer as the desktop, compiled to WebAssembly [1]. Sharing between existing users and within organisations stays on the desktop, with two-way sync [1].

**Why differences exist:** Each is **Cannot** (a browser can't do it), **Chosen** (we decided against it, usually for safety) or **Not yet** (ordinary remaining work) [1].

**Main differences:**
- No sign-in, orgs, or own workspace, and no two-way sync from a shared desk. A recipient's copy is a snapshot that reaches nobody [1].
- Most of the 46 widgets behave identically. Some are partly limited (e.g. markdown export, AI regeneration, CSV import) and some are unavailable: streamdeck and local-app-launcher (Cannot), agent (Chosen), image-gen, webhook, inbound-hook and attention (Not yet) [1].

- The Vault is always locked (Not yet, because its crypto is synchronous) [1].
- BYOK is Anthropic only, with the key held server-side [1].
- PlexiBrain semantic search and memory extraction from documents are unavailable (Chosen), and sending AI chat messages is not served yet [1].
- Working fine: drive, offline use, multiple tabs, AI via credits, calendar, focus tools and notifications [1].

**Coverage:** The browser serves 197 of the desktop's 529 channels. A full session of sign-up, desk creation, editing, upload and sharing needs only one missing channel, `mail:getAccount`, which cannot exist in a browser [1].

verdict.reason: The summary states the phased hybrid decision, the rejection of Option B and the phase details accurately, and lists all five ADR risks with mitigations, with nothing invented and a sensible, concise scope that leaves out the unrelated DRM addendum.

results.text:
**Decision:** Adopt a phased hybrid rather than replacing the browser wholesale. The browser is already real Chromium (`<webview>`), and the login failures came from fixable defects, chiefly a missing User-Agent [1]. The phases are: (1) harden `<webview>`, which is shipped and proven: clean UA, overlay `setActive` instead of `focusOn`, origin-gated autofill, and a permission denylist; (2) an external-browser OAuth handoff (`shell.openExternal` plus `haptyx://` and `session.cookies.set`/PKCE) for providers that block embedded browsers; (3) a native `WebContentsView` scoped to the focus/expand surface, with `session.loadExtension` for uBlock-Lite and Dark Reader; (4) screenshot-at-rest plus one pooled native view on activate, gated behind a spike. Phases 2-4 are proposed [1]. Option B, a wholesale native `WebContentsView` migration, is rejected because it would sacrifice smooth pan/zoom, clipping and layering [1].

**Main risks listed:**
- The UA regex could mangle the version string. This is mitigated by unit tests and idempotence [1].
- Some enterprise SSO blocks embedded browsers regardless of UA. Only Phase 2 fixes those; Phase 1 narrows the failures but does not eliminate them [1].
- Phase 4's native-view/CSS-transform sync is make-or-break. It needs a spike proving 60fps pan/zoom tracking and acceptable clipping; if the spike fails, stop at Phase 3 [1].
- The origin gate may be too strict for edge-case login domains. It fails closed, so autofill simply doesn't fire [1].
- Extension security: use a vetted shelf only, load specific reviewed builds, never arbitrary user-supplied extensions, and document the supported-API subset [1].

The extensions caveat is also stressed: Electron supports only a subset of the Chrome API, so the product should promise a vetted shelf, never Web-Store parity [1].
